extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism; editors, biographers, and literary historians
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and evaluative principles about composing, editing, and judging biography and edited editions of classic works, illustrated via the Life of Johnson and its editors. Emphasizes integrity of originals, biographical method, and what makes a biography valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for the integrity of original works
rubrics_metrics.description: Original works should be preserved rather than 'adulterated' by additions from other hands; additions made by another hand may grievously injure the general effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay condemns incorporations like Mr. Croker's insertion of passages from Sir John Hawkins and Mrs. Thrale into Boswell, and compares the folly to imagining Hume's History republished with large extracts from Pepys or Mrs. Hutchinson. Anti-pattern: producing editions that interpolate other authorities into a canonical narrative — this harms unity and harms the effect of a single mind working through material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer originals over modernized abridgments or 'rifacimenti'
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers intimate with a great original resent modernized reworkings, harmonies, abridgments, expurgated editions, or 'stage-copies' when the original is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: objections to 'cutting open' Milton or translating Bunyan into modern English; modernizing or abridging destroys the peculiar charm and unique flavor of the original. Practical rule: when possible, present or consult the original text rather than heavily adapted or expurgated versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial character as essential to a biography's interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A biography that displays the subject's character on every page has a delightful and sustaining interest; the personal stamp of the writer (or subject, in collected conversation) makes passages valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay argues Boswell's Life is so compelling because the writer's character is displayed throughout: this 'display of character' converts otherwise trivial passages into material of deep interest. For biographers: foreground the subject's personality; let the character shine through the narrative rather than smoothing it away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidness and frank self-exposure increase dramatic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Unstudied frankness — publishing the little vanities, follies, and oddities — can be dramatically effective and produce trustworthiness; Boswell's candidness is contrasted with Rousseau and Byron, whom he suggests wrote with effect in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay praises Boswell's perfect frankness: weaknesses others hide, he paraded, making his work resemble 'the conversation of the inmates of the Palace of Truth.' Guidance for memoirists/biographers: candid detail (even unflattering) can enhance authenticity and dramatic interest. Anti-pattern: calculated self-exposure intended only for effect is less trustworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation and retentive memory are key biographer skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick observation and retentive memory are crucial qualities for a biographer; such faculties can compensate for lack of other conventional talents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay notes Boswell's quick observation and retentive memory as the practical talents that made his work 'immortal.' Editors and evaluators should value accurate recollection of conversation and detail as central to good biography, even if the biographer lacks rhetorical polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: A biographer's personal weaknesses can enrich the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal failings (officiousness, inquisitiveness, impertinence, vanity) may supply the very qualities that make a biographical work unique and excellent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay asserts that were Boswell not a fool, he would not have produced his great book; his weaknesses provided material and dramatic interest. Practical implication: do not reflexively censor or suppress a biographer's idiosyncratic voice when it yields insight into the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial respect: avoid attacking the original author/biographer while annotating
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors who supply extensive notes should not simultaneously disparage the author whose text they are elucidating; excessive annotation coupled with contempt for the biographer is unsympathetic and inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay cites Mr. Croker, who published 2,500 notes yet 'scarcely ever mentions the biographer... without some expression of contempt.' Guidance for editors: annotations should illuminate and preserve the dignity of the original work; attacking the writer undermines editorial purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of domestic and behavioral minutiae to render intimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute details of appearance, habits, mannerisms, and domestic life (coat, wig, appetite, gestures, household characters) make a subject as familiar to readers as everyday objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay's long catalogue of Johnson's externals (wig, st. vitus's dance, orange-peel scraps, cat Hodge, negro Frank) exemplifies how such particulars produce an intimate portrait. For biographers: include vivid, small-scale details to animate the subject and ground reputation in concrete particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness across life stages strengthens biography
rubrics_metrics.description: A biographer who knows the subject mainly in later life lacks minute information about formative years; comprehensive familiarity across life stages better reveals how character became fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay points out Boswell and Mrs. Thrale first met Johnson after he was fifty; thus they could not inform us about his earlier development. Guidance: for authoritative biography seek sources or testimony covering youth, middle years, and old age; acknowledge gaps where present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional literary talents are not the sole metric of a biographer's value
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic, eloquence, wit, and taste — ordinary qualities prized in authors — may be absent in a biographer who nonetheless produces a great work through other faculties like memory and observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay observes Boswell lacks remarks of consequence on literature or politics yet achieves eminence. Evaluators should weigh non-traditional virtues (verisimilitude, candor, documentary detail) alongside classical literary criteria when judging biography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate evaluation of a work and the author's personal worth
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible to admire a book while holding contempt for its author; the book and the author need not be appraised identically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay calls Boswell's case 'an exception' where the work is universally admired although the man is broadly despised. Practical implication: critical assessment can and sometimes should treat textual achievement independently of the author's character or reputation.
